14990:
"Splash out" means to spend a noticeably large amount of money on something, especially as a treat — for yourself or for someone else. The key idea is that you are spending more than you normally would, and you are doing it willingly, often to enjoy or celebrate something.

It is a phrasal verb, which means two words ("splash" + "out") work together as a single unit with one meaning.

This is important, because the feeling of a phrase tells you when and how to use it correctly.

"Splash out" is not negative. It does not suggest foolishness or irresponsibility (unlike "throw money away" or "waste money"). Instead, it carries a warm, slightly indulgent tone — the sense that you have decided to treat yourself or someone else, and you feel good about it. There is often an element of occasion to it: a birthday, an anniversary, a holiday, a celebration, or simply the feeling that you deserve something nice.

Think of it like this: if you normally buy a ₹200 cup of coffee but one day you go to a fancy café and spend ₹800, you have splashed out. You knew it was expensive. You chose to do it anyway. And you probably felt it was worth it.
Grammar: How to Build Sentences With It

The basic structure

splash out + on + [the thing you spent money on]

This is the most common and natural way to use it.

  • She splashed out on a beautiful silk saree.
  • We splashed out on a five-star hotel for our anniversary.
  • He splashed out on the latest phone even though his old one worked fine.

Without specifying what you spent on

You can also use "splash out" on its own, without saying what you spent on, especially if it is already clear from context.

  • "Should we get the cheap seats?" "No, let's splash out."
  • It was our last night in Paris, so we decided to splash out.

With "for" (spending on behalf of someone)

Less commonly, you will see "splash out for" when you are spending generously on behalf of someone else.

  • Her parents really splashed out for her wedding.
  • He splashed out for his whole team when they won the contract.

Notice that "on" is about the item, while "for" is about the person.

Tenses

Like any verb, it changes form depending on tense:

  • Present: She always splashes out when she travels.
  • Past: We splashed out on dinner last night.
  • Continuous: They are splashing out on a new car.
  • Future: I am going to splash out on some new books this weekend.
  • Noun form (less common): It was a bit of a splash-out, but worth it.

Here are varied, natural examples to show you the full range of how this phrase is used:

  1. After months of saving, she splashed out on a weekend trip to Goa.
  2. The company splashed out on a lavish New Year party for all its employees.
  3. I don't usually spend much on shoes, but I splashed out on these — they are so comfortable.
  4. "Why did you buy such an expensive coffee machine?" "I just felt like splashing out."
  5. They splashed out on fresh flowers and candles to make the dinner feel special.
  6. He rarely spends on himself, but he splashed out for his son's graduation.
  7. The government splashed out on new infrastructure for the city.

Notice something across all these examples: in every case, the spending is deliberate and more than usual. No one is tricked into it. No one regrets it (at least, not in the moment of saying this phrase). It is a choice — sometimes extravagant, always intentional.
Where Does the Phrase Come From?

The word "splash" evokes the image of water being thrown about freely and without restraint — it goes everywhere, it cannot be controlled or reclaimed once it lands. When applied to money, it suggests spending in that same free, generous, unrestrained way.

"Out" adds the sense of something going away from you — your money is going out of your wallet and into the world. Together, "splash out" gives a vivid picture: money flying freely, like water being splashed.

"Splash out" is primarily British and Australian English. If you are reading a British novel, watching a British television show, or speaking with someone from the UK or Australia, you will hear this phrase often. It is very natural there.

In American English, the equivalent phrase is usually "splurge" (sometimes written as "splurge on something"). The meaning is almost identical.

  • British: We splashed out on a lovely dinner.
  • American: We splurged on a lovely dinner.

If you are speaking with Americans, "splash out" will still be understood, but it may sound slightly unfamiliar to them. "Splurge" is safer in an American context. In British, Australian, and Indian English contexts (India is heavily influenced by British English), "splash out" is perfectly natural.

It helps to know what this phrase does not mean, so you do not confuse it with similar ideas.

  • It does not mean you are being reckless or irresponsible with money (unlike "blow all your money on something").
  • It does not mean you spent all the money you have (unlike "break the bank," which is an exaggeration, or "spend your last penny").
  • It does not mean you are rich. Even someone with very modest means can "splash out" — it simply means they spent more than their usual amount on something.
  • It does not mean the purchase was a mistake. The phrase is neutral-to-positive. If someone regretted spending, they would more likely say they wasted money or threw money away, not that they "splashed out."

Understanding related phrases will deepen your grasp of "splash out":

  • Splurge (on) — the American equivalent; almost identical in meaning and tone.
  • Treat yourself (to) — spend money on something nice for yourself; softer and more gentle in tone, can apply to smaller amounts.
  • Go all out — do something in a big, extravagant way; not only about money, but can include effort and energy too.
  • Push the boat out — another British phrase meaning to spend generously or be extravagant, often in a social setting.
  • Spare no expense — spend as much as necessary without worrying about cost; slightly more formal and usually about a specific event.
  • Blow the budget — spend more than you planned; this one has a slightly more negative feel than "splash out."

Of these, "splash out" and "splurge" are the closest pair — nearly interchangeable, just separated by geography.

What it meansTo spend a noticeably large amount of money on something, as a treat
ToneWarm, indulgent, positive
Most common formsplash out on something
GeographyMainly British and Australian English
American equivalentSplurge
RegisterInformal, everyday speech

That is everything you need to know about "splash out." The next time you see it in a book, hear it in a show, or want to use it yourself, you will know exactly what it means, how it feels, and how to use it correctly.
14991: A splat is what happens — and what you see and hear — when something soft, wet, or liquid hits a hard surface suddenly and with enough force to spread out flat. It captures three things at once: the sound, the visual result, and the event itself.

1. The Sound

A splat is a specific kind of noise — a sharp, wet, smacking sound. It is not a bang (which is dry and hard), and not a splash (which suggests something falling into liquid). A splat is the sound of something soft or wet colliding flatly with a solid surface.

Think of:

  • A raw egg dropping on a kitchen floor
  • A wet cloth being slapped against a wall
  • A raindrop hitting a car roof

Each of those makes a "splat."

2. The Mark Left Behind

A splat also refers to the mess or stain that remains on the surface after the impact — the flattened, spread-out blob. Because soft or liquid things don't just hit and bounce; they spread outward in all directions from the point of impact.

For example, if a tomato is thrown at a wall, the smeared, irregular patch of red pulp left on the wall is the splat.

3. The Event Itself

"Splat" can also describe the whole incident — the moment of impact as a single event.

"The water balloon hit the ground with a splat."

Here, "a splat" means the entire occurrence: the fall, the impact, the sound, and the mess — all bundled into one word.
An Everyday Example to Tie It Together

Imagine you are holding a scoop of ice cream. It slips off the cone and falls onto the pavement.

  • The sound it makes when it hits — that wet, flat thwack — is a splat.
  • The spread-out, squashed blob of ice cream now sitting flat on the pavement is a splat.
  • The moment it happened — you can describe it as: "It fell with a splat."
What Makes "Splat" Different from Similar Words

WordKey difference
SplashInvolves liquid flying outward in drops, often into or from water. A splash is more explosive and scattered.
SmackA sharp slapping sound, but dry — no wetness or spreading implied.
ThudA heavy, dull impact sound — but solid and compact, not spreading or wet.
SplatterRelated to splat, but a splatter involves many droplets or pieces flying off in multiple directions. A splat is more of a single, contained impact.

A splat is uniquely about wetness or softness + a flat surface + spreading outward. Remove any of those qualities, and it becomes a different word.

In Furniture

In chair-making, the splat (also called a chair splat) is the flat, wide, vertical panel in the centre of a chair's back — the piece that runs up the middle between the seat and the top rail of the backrest. It is so named because it resembles a flat, spread-out shape, much like a splat of something squashed flat.

In Computing (Informal)

In programmer and hacker culture, particularly in older computing communities, the asterisk symbol (\) is sometimes informally called a "splat." This is because the asterisk looks visually like something that has been squashed flat and spread outward — like a splat. You might hear a programmer say *"put a splat before the variable name" to mean "put an asterisk there."

"Splat" is an onomatopoeic word — meaning the word itself sounds like what it describes. When you say "splat" aloud, the short, flat, sudden sound of the word mirrors the sudden, flat impact it describes. This is why it feels so natural and satisfying to use. Your mouth even makes a small "smacking" motion to say it.

A splat is (1) the wet, flat smacking sound of something soft hitting a hard surface, (2) the spread-out mark or mess left after that impact, and (3) the event of that impact itself. In furniture, it refers to the central flat panel in a chair back. In computing slang, it means the asterisk (*) symbol.
14992:
To splay something means to spread it outward, wide apart, and often at an angle — usually in a way that feels stretched, flat, or ungainly.

Think of a hand pressed hard against a surface, with every finger pushed as far away from every other finger as possible. That's splaying. The movement is outward and apart, and it typically involves some force or extreme extension.
The Three Main Ways It's Used

1. Spreading body parts wide apart

This is the most common, everyday use. You splay limbs, fingers, or toes when you extend them outward as far as they can go — often in a loose, uncontrolled, or deliberate way.

  • A cat stretched out in the sun, with all four legs pushed out flat in every direction, has splayed its legs.
  • A child pressing their hand into wet paint, fingers pushed as wide as possible, is splaying their fingers.
  • A person who trips and lands face-down on the floor, arms and legs thrown outward, has splayed across the floor.

Notice the feeling here: it's not a small, careful movement. It suggests something going wide, flat, and outward — often with a lack of elegance.

2. A whole body spreading out or collapsing outward

When a person or creature falls, collapses, or relaxes onto a surface and their body spreads out in all directions, we say they splay or are splayed out.

  • "He was exhausted. He just splayed across the couch and didn't move for an hour."
  • "The body was found splayed on the ground."

This sense carries a strong visual: the image of something going limp and spreading wide, like a starfish dropped on a surface.

3. In architecture — an angled, widening cut or opening

This is a more technical use, but worth knowing. In buildings, a window or doorway is sometimes splayed — meaning the sides of the wall opening are cut at an angle, so the opening is wider on one side (usually the interior) than the other. This was done historically to let more light into a room through a thick stone wall.

The same principle applies in carpentry: a splayed cut is a cut made at a slant rather than straight, so a surface widens as it goes outward.

"Splay" almost always carries a visual quality of something opening up wide in a way that is either:

  • Forceful (fingers splayed wide with pressure)
  • Loose and limp (a body splayed in exhaustion or death)
  • Structurally deliberate (an opening splayed to create a wider angle)

It almost never describes a small or neat movement. There's always a sense of going to the extreme edges, of things being pushed or stretched as far out as they go.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Spread is the general word — neutral and very broad. You spread butter, you spread a map. Splay is more specific: it implies a wide, outward, often angular or awkward movement — usually of something with limbs, joints, or edges.

Sprawl is close but describes a whole body lying in a loose, disorganized way, usually horizontally. Splay focuses more on the act of pushing parts outward and apart, while sprawl describes the resulting posture.

Stretch implies extension in one direction, usually to reach something. Splay implies extension in multiple outward directions simultaneously — apart, wide, fanned out.
A Range of Sentences to Cement It

• "The surgeon splayed the tissue back to expose the area beneath." (pushed it wide open and apart)
  • "She splayed her toes in the warm sand." (spread them wide and outward)
  • "The frog splayed its legs as it landed." (they spread out flat to either side)
  • "He lay splayed on his back in the grass, staring at the clouds." (body spread wide and loose)
  • "The window was splayed outward to draw in more light." (angled to widen)
  • "The impact splayed the metal outward from the center of the dent." (forced it out and apart)

If you had to remember just one definition: to splay is to push or spread something outward, wide, and apart — often in a way that is angular, flat, or ungainly, like fingers pressed hard against glass or limbs thrown out in a fall.
14993: The word spleen carries two distinct meanings — one literal and one figurative. Both are in active use, so knowing both is essential.

A spleen is an organ inside the human (and animal) body. It sits in the upper-left part of your belly, tucked just behind your stomach, roughly the size of your fist.

It is not as famous as the heart or lungs, but it does quiet, important work:

  • It filters your blood. Think of it as a quality-control inspector. It continuously scans your blood and pulls out red blood cells that are old, damaged, or misshapen. Without this, worn-out cells would pile up in your bloodstream.
  • It is part of your immune system. The spleen stores and deploys white blood cells — the soldiers your body sends out to fight infections. When you get sick, your spleen can swell up slightly because it's working harder.
  • It acts as a small blood reservoir. In emergencies (like sudden blood loss), the spleen can squeeze out a reserve of blood to help the body cope.

Important facts worth knowing:

  • A ruptured spleen is a serious medical emergency, usually caused by a hard blow to the abdomen (a car accident, a sports injury). Because the spleen holds a lot of blood, a rupture can cause dangerous internal bleeding and requires immediate medical attention.
  • You can live without your spleen. Doctors can remove it (this surgery is called a splenectomy) if it's severely damaged or diseased. People who have had their spleen removed generally live normal lives, but they become slightly more vulnerable to certain bacterial infections for the rest of their lives, and may need vaccines or preventive antibiotics as a precaution.
  • An enlarged spleen (medically called splenomegaly) can happen with infections like mononucleosis (glandular fever), liver disease, or certain blood disorders. Doctors check for it by feeling the abdomen.

Example sentences (literal meaning):

  • "The doctor was concerned that the injury might have damaged his spleen."
  • "An ultrasound showed that her spleen was slightly enlarged due to the infection."
Meaning 2: Bad Temper, Spite, or Bitter Anger (Figurative)

This is the literary and formal meaning of the word. When used this way, spleen means a feeling of irritable bad temper, bitter resentment, or spiteful anger — especially the kind that someone has been building up inside and then explosively releases.

It's not everyday casual anger. It carries a sense of something pent-up, sharp, and somewhat unpleasant to witness.

The key phrase to know:

"To vent one's spleen" is the most common expression using this meaning. It means to release your pent-up frustration, anger, or bitterness — often by saying harsh or critical things.

  • "After years of being overlooked, he finally vented his spleen in a long, scathing letter to management."
  • "She didn't mean to take it out on her friend — she was simply venting her spleen after a terrible week."

Standalone use:

You'll also see "spleen" used on its own in this sense, particularly in older or formal writing:

  • "He spoke with barely concealed spleen, his voice tight with resentment."
  • "The critic's review was full of spleen — it felt less like analysis and more like a personal attack."
How the Two Meanings Connect (Without Going into History)

It is worth knowing that the figurative meaning is not random — ancient thinkers genuinely believed the spleen (the organ) was the physical seat of anger and dark emotions in the body. So when you see "spleen" used to mean irritability or spite, it's a direct carryover of that old belief, now fossilised into the language as a figure of speech. The organ and the emotion were once considered the same thing; today we know they aren't, but the word stuck.
Putting It All Together: How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

ContextMeaning

It's usually easy to tell from context:

  • If the sentence is about a body, injury, illness, anatomy, or medicine, the organ is meant.
  • If the sentence is about anger, bitterness, frustration, or emotional outbursts, the figurative meaning is meant.
  • If you see "vent one's spleen" anywhere, it is always figurative — always.

Spleen as a noun means:

  1. A fist-sized organ in the upper-left abdomen that filters blood, stores immune cells, and can be life-threatening if ruptured.
  2. Bitter, pent-up anger or bad temper — especially as expressed outwardly. Most commonly seen in the phrase "vent one's spleen."

The first meaning is used in medical and everyday contexts. The second is more literary and formal, but widely understood by educated speakers and commonly seen in writing, journalism, and literature.
14994:
Splendid means something is impressively excellent, beautiful, or magnificent — so good or striking that it fills you with admiration or delight. It describes something that truly stands out in a very positive way.

Think of it this way: if "good" is a thumbs up, then "splendid" is a standing ovation.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. Describing Something Visually Grand or Beautiful

Here, "splendid" describes something that looks breathtaking, magnificent, or dazzlingly impressive to the eye.

"The king lived in a splendid palace decorated with gold and marble."
"The sunset over the ocean was absolutely splendid."
"The guests arrived in splendid costumes for the grand ball."

In this sense, "splendid" is not just "pretty." It means the kind of beautiful that makes you stop and stare.

2. Describing Something of Very High Quality or Excellence

Here, "splendid" has nothing to do with looks. It simply means that something is remarkably well done, highly valuable, or particularly good.

"She did a splendid job on the presentation."
"That was a splendid idea — let's go with it."
"He showed splendid courage during the crisis."

"Splendid" is not a cold or neutral word. It carries warmth and genuine enthusiasm. When you call something splendid, you are not just labelling it — you are expressing real admiration or delight. It has an uplifting, celebratory energy to it.

Compare these two sentences:

"The meal was adequate." — flat, no emotion.
"The meal was splendid." — enthusiastic, full of praise.

It is a genuinely strong word. Think of it on a scale like this:

okay → good → great → excellent / splendid → extraordinary / perfect

It sits comfortably in the upper range of praise. It is not the absolute maximum (you wouldn't use it for something that defies all human understanding), but it is real, high, sincere praise — not something you say casually about average things.

One of the most common uses of "splendid" is as a one-word exclamation of approval or satisfaction — similar to saying "Excellent!", "Wonderful!", or "Great!"

Someone says: "I've booked the tickets for tonight."
You reply: "Splendid! I can't wait."

This use is especially common in British English, where it sounds completely natural and warm. In American English, it may sound slightly formal or old-fashioned, but it is still perfectly understood and often used to give a response a classic, refined feel.

"Splendid" leans slightly formal and refined compared to words like "awesome," "fantastic," or "amazing." It has a certain elegance to it. You are more likely to see it in:

  • British English (where it is very common in everyday speech)
  • Formal writing (reviews, literature, speeches)
  • Polished, sophisticated conversation

That said, it is not stiff or stuffy — it can still feel warm and personal.

Yes, like most positive words, "splendid" can be used sarcastically in the right tone or context — meaning the opposite of what it says.

"My phone just died, and it's going to rain. Splendid."

Here, the speaker clearly does not mean it genuinely. However, this is not the word's natural meaning — sarcasm depends on tone and context, not the word itself.

These words are close cousins, but they are not identical:

  • Magnificent — focuses more on impressive scale or grandeur. A cathedral is magnificent. A kind gesture, not so much. "Splendid" works in both cases.
  • Excellent — equally strong praise for quality, but more neutral and businesslike. "Splendid" is warmer and more expressive.
  • Wonderful — also warm and emotional, but "wonderful" hints more at something that fills you with wonder. "Splendid" emphasizes a quality of impressiveness or brilliance.
  • Superb — strong, precise praise, but colder in tone. "Splendid" is more enthusiastic and celebratory.
  • Glorious — closer to "splendid" in warmth, but often used for things that feel triumphant, heroic, or spiritually uplifting. "Splendid" is broader.

What it meansImpressively excellent, beautiful, or magnificent
Main usesVisual grandeur OR high quality/excellence
Emotional toneWarm, enthusiastic, genuinely admiring
StrengthStrong praise — well above "good" or "nice"
RegisterSlightly formal/elegant; very common in British English
As exclamation"Splendid!" = "Excellent! / Wonderful!"
A Few More Example Sentences to Cement It

The orchestra gave a splendid performance that left the audience speechless.
What a splendid view of the mountains from up here!
She has a splendid mind — her reasoning is always sharp and clear.
The children were on splendid form at the competition.
"You've passed the exam!" — "Splendid! All that hard work paid off."

Once you truly understand "splendid," you will notice that it is the perfect word for those moments when something deserves more than a plain "good" — when something genuinely impresses you, delights you, or earns your wholehearted admiration.
14995:
Splendiferous means extraordinarily magnificent, impressively grand, or dazzlingly wonderful — something so beautiful, impressive, or excellent that ordinary words like "nice" or even "great" feel completely inadequate to describe it.

Think of it as a supercharged, dressed-up version of the word "splendid." If "splendid" is a single firework, "splendiferous" is an entire fireworks show.

What makes "splendiferous" special isn't just what it means — it's how it feels. The word carries genuine awe and excitement. When you call something splendiferous, you're not calmly approving of it — you're marveling at it. It also has a playful, theatrical, larger-than-life quality. It sounds like something a captivating storyteller or an enthusiastic child might say. On top of that, it has a slightly old-fashioned, whimsical charm — like something you might encounter in a Roald Dahl book or a classic adventure story.

On a scale of positive adjectives, splendiferous sits at the very top — beyond "good," "great," "wonderful," and even "splendid." It implies something that genuinely stops you in your tracks and makes you marvel.

This is important: the word works in two distinct ways, and knowing both will make you a fluent user of it.

The first is sincere use, when you genuinely want to express that something is extraordinarily magnificent: "The view from the mountaintop was absolutely splendiferous — I had never seen anything like it in my life."

The second is humorous or ironic use. Because of its dramatic, over-the-top sound, splendiferous is very commonly used in a lighthearted or tongue-in-cheek way — sometimes to describe everyday things with exaggerated enthusiasm: "My mother made her splendiferous lasagna again — the whole family went silent at the table." Or even: "After three days of eating nothing but plain crackers, a bowl of soup felt absolutely splendiferous."

This ironic use is actually extremely common and natural. The word's theatrical flair makes it a perfect fit for playful exaggeration.
When and where to use it

Splendiferous is an informal, literary word. It sits comfortably in casual conversation, creative writing, fiction, storytelling, humor, and children's literature. You would generally not use it in formal or professional writing — a business report, a legal document, or an academic paper — where a neutral, precise tone is expected. In those contexts, it would feel out of place.

"The birthday cake was nothing short of splendiferous — three tiers of chocolate, covered in golden flowers."

"He walked into the party wearing the most splendiferous hat anyone had ever seen."

"The old library was splendiferous, with floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, stained glass windows, and a winding spiral staircase."

"After a week of nothing but instant noodles, a proper home-cooked meal tasted splendiferous."
How it compares to similar words

"Splendid" is more formal and restrained — it approves without gushing. "Magnificent" is grand and impressive, often used for large-scale things like architecture or nature, but it is neutral in tone. "Glorious" suggests radiance and inspiring greatness. "Spectacular" emphasizes dramatic visual impact. "Wonderful" is warm but mild.

Splendiferous contains the essence of all of these, but adds something none of the others have: a sense of joyful, theatrical exuberance. It is the most personality-filled, expressive, and emotionally alive word of the group. Choosing "splendiferous" over "magnificent" tells the listener not just that something is impressive, but that you are delighted by it.

If you want to say something is magnificently, grandly, and dazzlingly wonderful — and you want to say it with personality, enthusiasm, warmth, and a touch of flair — splendiferous is your word. It means the very best kind of impressive, wrapped in a big, enthusiastic, slightly theatrical bow.
14996:
Splendor means a kind of beauty or greatness that is so impressive, so grand, and so striking that it immediately fills you with a sense of awe and wonder. It's not quiet, soft, or subtle beauty. It's the kind that hits you, stops you in your tracks, and makes you think, "Wow. I have never seen anything like this."

Think of the moment you stand at the edge of the Grand Canyon for the first time, or watch the sun sink below the ocean horizon in a blaze of gold and orange. That overwhelming, breathtaking feeling you get — the thing causing that feeling is splendor.

Splendor can describe three closely related but slightly different things:

1. Magnificent visual beauty
This is the most common use. Splendor describes something that looks breathtakingly grand, rich, or dazzling to the eye. It's beauty on a large, impressive scale.

  • "The tourists were speechless before the splendor of the Taj Mahal."
  • "She gazed at the splendor of the autumn forest — the reds, golds, and oranges stretching for miles."

2. Brilliant or radiant light
Splendor can also describe a powerful, glowing brightness — the kind that seems to radiate greatness.

  • "The splendor of the morning sun filled the entire valley."
  • "The stars shone with a splendor that city dwellers rarely see."

3. Glory, greatness, or remarkable impressiveness
This use goes beyond what you can see. It describes the peak greatness of something — an empire, a career, an era — when it was at its most powerful, celebrated, or impressive.

  • "Historians studied the splendor of the Roman Empire."
  • "The splendor of her musical career inspired a whole generation."

To truly understand splendor, you need to feel what separates it from ordinary beauty or greatness. Here's the key: splendor always has scale and force. It is never small, shy, or gentle. It commands your attention. It overwhelms your senses. It has a kind of presence.

A single red rose on a table is beautiful — but it is not splendor.
A vast rose garden in full bloom, stretching across rolling hills, glistening in the morning light — that is splendor.

A good speech is impressive — but it is not splendor.
A once-in-a-generation performance that moves an entire stadium to tears — that is splendor.

Splendor is beauty or greatness turned up to its highest volume.

• Splendor (singular) refers to the quality itself — the overall feeling or impression of magnificence.
    • "She was overwhelmed by the splendor of the palace."
  • Splendors (plural) refers to specific impressive or beautiful things within something larger — individual elements that together create that grandeur.
    • "The museum displayed the splendors of ancient Egypt — the jewels, the carvings, the golden masks."
    • "He traveled the world to witness the natural splendors of each continent."

You will see this word spelled two ways, and both are completely correct:

  • Splendor — used in American English
  • Splendour — used in British English

Same word. Same meaning. Just a spelling difference between the two versions of English.
Words That Are Similar — And How Splendor Differs From Them

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your feel for splendor:

Magnificence — Perhaps the closest synonym. Both words describe grand, impressive beauty. But magnificence leans more toward lavishness, richness, and luxury — the feeling of something built or created with great wealth and care. Splendor is broader; it applies equally to nature as to man-made things.

Grandeur — Focuses on sheer size, scale, and dignity. Something can have grandeur by being simply enormous and imposing (like a mountain range). Splendor adds the extra layer of beauty and brilliance — it dazzles, not just impresses.

Glory — Overlaps with splendor, but glory carries stronger meanings of honor, fame, and achievement. A soldier can earn glory in battle; a sunset has splendor, not glory (a sunset hasn't earned anything).

Majesty — Suggests dignity, power, and a commanding presence — often used for royalty or nature's most powerful scenes. Splendor is warmer and more connected to beauty; majesty is more about authority and scale.

One of the most important things to understand about splendor is that it is defined by the response it creates in the person experiencing it. Splendor is not a cold, clinical quality. Something has splendor because it produces awe, wonder, admiration, or even a kind of reverence in the person who encounters it.

This is why the word often appears in emotional, poetic, or descriptive writing. When a writer uses splendor, they are not just describing what something looks like — they are telling you how it felt to witness it.

Splendor is a formal and elevated word. It belongs to a higher register of language — the kind used in literature, formal writing, travel writing, history, and poetry. You would not use it in casual conversation the way you might use "awesome" or "stunning."

You would say: "The splendor of the cathedral left us breathless" in a travel article.
You would probably not say: "That pizza had real splendor" — that would sound strange and mismatched.

Use it when you want to describe something that is genuinely grand, beautiful, and impressive on a large scale, and when the context is thoughtful or formal enough to carry the weight of the word.

Splendor is the quality of being magnificently beautiful, brilliantly bright, or impressively great — on a scale that produces awe and wonder in those who witness it. It can describe the grandeur of nature, the richness of architecture and art, the radiance of light, or the peak greatness of a civilization or era. It is always large in feeling, never subtle, and always makes a powerful impression.
14997:
If someone is splenetic, they are deeply, habitually bad-tempered, bitter, and prone to angry, sharp outbursts. Think of it as a kind of poisonous grumpiness — not a passing mood, but a persistent state of irritability mixed with spite and scorn.

A splenetic person doesn't just get annoyed. They seethe. They bristle. They lash out with a sour, cutting edge to their words, and they seem to carry a chip on their shoulder at all times.

The word captures a very specific flavor of bad temper. It combines three things at once:

  • Chronic irritability — they are always like this, not just having a bad day.
  • Bitterness — there's a resentful, sour quality to their anger, as if they feel wronged by the world.
  • Sharpness — their anger tends to come out as cutting remarks, harsh criticism, or angry tirades rather than, say, quiet sulking.

A splenetic person is not someone who cries in frustration. They're more likely to fire off a contemptuous, venomous comment, write a furious letter, or go on a blistering rant. There's an energy and a sting to their bad temper.

The word can describe:

  • A person: "He was a splenetic old critic who despised nearly every book ever written."
  • A tone or mood: "She responded in a splenetic mood, snapping at everyone in the office."
  • Writing or speech: "The newspaper column was a splenetic attack on the mayor's every decision."
  • A rant or outburst: "He delivered a splenetic tirade against modern music."

Notice that when applied to writing or speech, it means the content itself is angry, bitter, and sharply critical — not just mildly disapproving.

Splenetic sits at the strong end of the bad-temper spectrum. Consider this rough scale:

Grumpy → Irritable → Peevish → Cantankerous → Splenetic

  • Grumpy and irritable are everyday words for someone who's in a sour mood — perhaps anyone on a bad day.
  • Peevish adds a slightly childish, petty quality to the annoyance.
  • Cantankerous suggests someone who is stubbornly argumentative and difficult to deal with.
  • Splenetic goes further — it implies a bitterness, a venom, and a habitual quality that makes it one of the strongest words in this family.
How It Differs From Its Closest Cousins

Nearby wordHow it differs from "splenetic"

Irascible means someone who gets angry very quickly and easily. It's about the quickness of their temper. Splenetic is more about the ongoing bitterness and sting.

Choleric also means quick to anger and hot-headed. Again, it's about the speed of the flare-up. Splenetic is darker and more sustained.

Bilious is perhaps the closest cousin — bitter, bad-tempered, and unpleasant — but splenetic tends to be more specifically associated with angry, harsh expression and criticism.

Caustic describes sharp, cutting words or remarks, but doesn't necessarily imply bad temper or bitterness as a personality trait.

Splenetic uniquely packages: habitual bad temper + deep-seated bitterness + a sharp, venomous expression of that anger, often in the form of attacks or criticism.
The Register: When and Where You'll See This Word

Splenetic is a fairly formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday speech much. You're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Literary criticism or book reviews
  • Sophisticated journalism or opinion writing
  • Classic or literary fiction
  • Academic writing about history, politics, or culture

When a writer uses "splenetic," they are making a deliberate, precise word choice. It signals that the bad temper being described is not mild or passing — it is intense, bitter, and characteristically sharp.

• "The professor was known for his splenetic response to any student who challenged his theories."
  • "She wrote a splenetic review that tore apart the film without a single moment of generosity."
  • "Years of disappointment had turned him splenetic — he found fault in everything and everyone."
  • "The politician's splenetic outburst shocked even his closest allies."

If you need to anchor this word in your memory with a single image: picture a bitter, sharp-tongued old critic — someone whose default expression is a sneer, who always has a cutting remark ready, and who seems to resent the world around them. That person is splenetic.

To splice means to join two things together at their ends — in a way that makes them feel like one continuous, unbroken thing. The key idea is not just joining things (like tying a knot or using a clip), but weaving, overlapping, or fusing them so that the connection is strong, smooth, and often nearly invisible.

Think of it this way: if you have two short ropes and you want one long rope, you could simply tie them together — but a knot creates a bulge and a weak point. Splicing is the skilled alternative: you unravel the ends of both ropes, interweave their individual strands together, and the result is a single seamless rope. That process — joining by interweaving or carefully overlapping the ends — is the heart of what "splice" means.

Before diving into contexts, it helps to understand what makes splicing splicing, and not just "joining" or "connecting."

1. It happens at the ends. You splice the end of one thing to the end of another. You're not slapping two things side by side; you're extending one into the other.

2. The goal is continuity. The result should ideally behave as one single, uninterrupted thing — not two things held together.

3. It requires skill and precision. Splicing is a deliberate, careful act. It's the opposite of a sloppy fix.

4. It often involves interlocking or interweaving. This is what makes the join strong and seamless.

The word "splice" is used in several different fields, and understanding each one will cement the meaning in your mind.

Ropes and cables (the original meaning)
This is where the word comes from and what it most literally describes. Sailors and sailors have long needed to join ropes permanently. To splice a rope, you unravel the stranded ends of both ropes and then weave those strands into each other. The result is a join that is often stronger than the rope itself. You can also splice a rope back onto itself to form a loop — called an eye splice.

Film and audio tape
Before digital editing existed, film editors worked with actual physical strips of film or magnetic audio tape. To create a final film or recording, they would cut the strips and literally splice them — meaning they would carefully align the cut ends and join them, usually with a special adhesive tape, so the film or audio played as one continuous piece. This is why the editing room was sometimes called a "splicing room," and even today the word survives in digital audio software, where editors still talk about splicing audio tracks.

Genetics and biology
This is one of the most important modern uses of the word. In biology, scientists can splice DNA — meaning they cut a strand of DNA and insert a piece of genetic material from another source into it, then rejoin the ends. The result is a new, combined strand of DNA that carries genes from two different origins. This is the foundation of genetic engineering. The phrase "gene splicing" is very common. There is also a natural biological process called RNA splicing, where the cell itself removes unnecessary sections from a strand of RNA and joins the remaining pieces back together into a continuous, working strand.

Woodworking and construction
When two lengths of timber or structural beams need to be joined end-to-end to create a longer piece, carpenters splice them — by cutting overlapping shapes into the ends (like a diagonal cut or a stepped cut) and fitting them together, then fastening them. This gives the joint much greater strength than a simple flat butt-join would.

Electrical wiring
Electricians splice wires when they join the bare end of one wire to the bare end of another. This might mean twisting the copper strands together and securing them, or using a connector. The goal is a continuous flow of electricity through what behaves as a single wire.

Outside of technical fields, people also use "splice" more loosely to mean joining or combining two things in a way that blends them together. For example:

  • "The director spliced two storylines together skillfully." — meaning the two separate plot threads were woven together so that they felt unified.
  • "The remix splices elements of jazz and electronic music." — meaning the two styles are interleaved, not just placed one after the other.

In informal British English, the phrase "get spliced" is a lighthearted way of saying "get married" — the idea being that two people are being joined together as one.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Join / connect — These are general words. They just mean bringing two things together. They say nothing about how. Splice is specific: it tells you the method involves interweaving or overlapping the ends.
  • Tie — Tying creates a fastening at a point, but the two things remain distinct and the knot is a separate element. Splicing aims to make the join invisible and integral.
  • Attach / fasten — These words imply one thing being fixed onto another. Splicing implies two things becoming one.
  • Merge — Merge is about two things becoming one, but is usually abstract (companies merge, lanes merge). Splice is more physical and technical, and implies a specific technique of end-to-end joining.

These will help you see the word in action:

  • "The sailor spliced the two ropes together before lowering the anchor."
  • "The editor spliced the scene from Tuesday's shoot into the beginning of the film."
  • "Scientists spliced the insulin-producing gene into bacterial DNA to produce the medicine."
  • "The electrician spliced the broken wire and wrapped it in insulating tape."
  • "The composer spliced recordings of street noise into the symphony's opening."
  • "They decided to get spliced in a small ceremony by the sea." (informal, = get married)

If you had to carry just one idea in your head: to splice is to join two things end-to-end by interweaving or carefully fusing them together, so that the result behaves as one continuous, seamless whole.
14999: A splinter is a small, thin, sharp piece that has broken off or separated from a larger solid object. Think of it as a fragment — but not just any fragment. A splinter is specifically thin, needle-like, and usually pointed at one or both ends. That sharp, shard-like shape is what makes a splinter a splinter, and not just a "piece" or "chunk."

Imagine snapping a dry stick in half. Along the broken edge, you might notice tiny, thin, sharp needles of wood sticking out or falling off. Those are splinters. They are:

  • Long and narrow (not blocky or round)
  • Sharp at the tip (like a tiny spike or needle)
  • Thin (sometimes thin enough to be nearly invisible)
  • Small (usually just a few millimetres to a couple of centimetres long)

Wood is by far the most common source, but splinters can come from almost any hard, brittle material that breaks apart in a sharp, shard-like way:

  • Wood — rough wooden planks, old furniture, tree bark, wooden fences
  • Glass — shattered glass breaks into thin, razor-sharp splinters
  • Metal — certain metals, when fractured, produce fine, sharp fragments
  • Bone — in medical situations, a broken bone can produce splinters
  • Plastic — hard, brittle plastics can snap into shard-like splinters
The Most Familiar Scenario — A Splinter in Your Skin

This is where most people first encounter the word. If you run your hand along a rough, unfinished wooden surface — an old park bench, a wooden plank, a fence — a tiny pointed sliver of wood can pierce your skin and get stuck underneath it. That is a splinter.

It sits just below the surface of your skin, you can sometimes see it, and it causes a sharp, stinging pain, especially when you press on that spot. Getting it out usually requires a pair of tweezers or a needle. Almost everyone has experienced this, which is why "splinter" is so strongly associated with wood and skin.
Splinters in a Wider Physical Sense

Beyond skin and wood, you will also hear "splinter" used for any thin, sharp fragment of a shattered hard material. For example:

  • When a glass window shatters violently, splinters of glass fly outward.
  • A bomb or explosion can send splinters of metal (also called shrapnel) in all directions.
  • A falling mirror might leave splinters scattered across the floor.

In all these cases, the key idea is the same: a thin, sharp, dangerous fragment that has broken off from something solid.
The Figurative Meaning — When "Splinter" Describes Groups or Organizations

This is where the word moves beyond the physical world. Just as a splinter breaks away from a larger piece of wood, the word "splinter" is used to describe a small group of people that breaks away from a larger group, usually because of disagreements or differences in beliefs.

This usage gives rise to the very common phrase "splinter group" — a faction that separates itself from a larger organization, political party, religion, or movement.

After years of internal conflict, a small splinter group broke away from the main political party and formed their own.

The religious splinter group rejected the teachings of the main church.

The image is deliberate and powerful — just like a physical splinter, these groups are smaller, sharper (in their views), and separated from the main body.
Quick Summary of All Its Meanings

SenseIn Simple Terms
Physical (most common)A small, thin, sharp piece broken off from a larger solid object (wood, glass, metal, etc.)
MedicalA sharp fragment lodged under the skin
FigurativeA small group that has broken away from a larger one

• She winced as she pulled a splinter from her thumb.
  • The wooden floor was old and full of splinters.
  • Splinters of glass covered the pavement after the car accident.
  • A splinter of the original movement formed their own independent group.
  • He used tweezers to carefully remove the splinter embedded in his heel.

If you ever need to recall the word fast: a splinter is a thin, sharp, pointed fragment — most often wood — that has broken away from something larger, sometimes embedding itself painfully in skin, and (figuratively) any small, sharp faction that breaks off from a larger whole.
